AI CLI Tools Community Digest 2026-11-14

Generated: 2026-11-14 01:24 UTC | Tools covered: 7

  • Claude Code
  • OpenAI Codex
  • Gemini CLI
  • GitHub Copilot CLI
  • OpenCode
  • Pi
  • Qwen Code
  • Claude Code Skills

Cross-Tool Comparison

Cross-Tool Comparison Report: AI CLI Ecosystem

Data window: 2026-11-14 | Tools: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Pi, Qwen Code

1. Ecosystem Overview

The AI CLI tooling landscape has consolidated around a shared set of hard problems — destructive-command safety, credential hygiene, subagent reliability, and cross-platform (especially Windows) stability — even as each tool pursues distinct architectural bets. Release cadence remains high: Codex, Copilot CLI, and OpenCode all shipped stable releases within the window, while Claude Code pushed a security patch and Gemini CLI entered a quiet stabilization phase with no releases. A clear bifurcation is emerging between first-party vendor tools (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI) optimizing for deep integration with their own model ecosystems, and independent aggregators (OpenCode, Pi, Qwen Code) competing on provider-agnostic routing, plugin/SDK extensibility, and multi-channel deployment. Across all communities, users are hitting the limits of single-session, single-surface agent workflows and demanding continuity, observability, and finer lifecycle control. Security and data-loss reports are no longer isolated — they form recurring bug classes rather than one-offs, signaling that guardrail architecture is now a first-order competitive differentiator.

2. Activity Comparison

Tool Hot Issues (today) PRs Updated (24h) Discussions Release Status (24h)
Claude Code 10 notable (2 filed today; 2 new data-loss incidents) 1 (near-empty pipeline) N/A (not provided) v2.1.325 patch (zstd security fix)
OpenAI Codex 10 notable (Windows auth dominant) ~14 (mostly copyberry[bot], closed same-day) 7 active (Ideas/Q&A/Show-and-tell) rust-v0.169.0 + v0.168.0 stable; v0.171 alphas
Gemini CLI 10 notable (P1 subagent bugs) 10 (security/sandbox heavy) N/A (not provided) None
GitHub Copilot CLI 10 notable + 3 honorable mentions 2 (both Dependabot, closed) N/A (not provided) v1.0.111 + v1.0.112 patch
OpenCode 10 notable (366-comment free-tier mega-thread) 10 (accessibility, session hygiene) N/A (not provided) v2.3.0 (background subagents; regressions reported)
Pi 10 notable (retry/resilience cluster) 7 (all closed; stability-focused) 3 (Show-and-tell/projects) None
Qwen Code 10 notable (CI flakes dominate) 10 (feature fixes + CI deflake) N/A (not provided) None

Notes:

  • N/A in Discussions indicates no Discussion data was supplied for that repo in the source digests — this reflects reporting scope, not channel inactivity. GitHub Issues/PRs remain the primary channel for Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI, OpenCode, and Qwen Code.
  • Pi's issue/PR links were provided without full URLs; counts reflect the digest's top-10 lists.

3. Shared Feature Directions

Several requirements recur across three or more communities, making them the clearest industry-level signals:

A. Destructive-command guardrails & safer execution

  • Claude Code: rm -rf, rsync --delete, malformed pkill incidents (##95426, #109735, #109627) — top pain point, explicitly called "overdue" for variable-expansion validation.
  • Gemini CLI: models reaching for git reset --force; workspace pollution (#22672, #23571); sandbox permission denial gaps (#30277).
  • OpenCode: agent continued after explicit STOP, unauthorized file modification (#63216).
  • Shared need: pre-execution validation of variable expansion, configurable allowlists, and reliable kill/containment semantics.

B. Credential hygiene — move secrets out of plaintext

  • Claude Code: OS secret store request, 👍11 (#73582); plaintext tokens under ~/.claude/.
  • Codex: shell snapshots persisting secret env vars in plaintext (#30971).
  • Copilot CLI: Entra token cache stays 0 bytes after MCP sign-in (#5236, closed); sandboxed git credential injection (#5102, closed).
  • Shared need: first-class OS keychain integration and MCP-derived token isolation.

C. Subagent reliability, observability & lifecycle control

  • Gemini CLI: false-success reporting (status: "success" on MAX_TURNS, #22323), hangs (#21409), Wayland failures (#21983), subagent traces via /chat share (#22598).
  • OpenCode: sessionID continuation broken (#59293), suspend/resume request 👍18 (#27511), model-call failures (#63778).
  • Pi: orphaned subagent children on quit (#12130, closed).
  • Qwen Code: continuable subagents (#16518); loop-stop semantics (#15894).
  • Shared need: truthful status reporting, hierarchical token accounting, and pause/resume.

D. Cross-surface session continuity

  • Codex: "continuous engineering workspace" (#61348), address existing conversations (#49862), verify thread startup state (#61177).
  • Copilot CLI: --host-allow-session-creation for remote hosts (v1.0.111).
  • Claude Code: phone-initiated remote sessions (#91815, 👍14).
  • Shared need: sessions that are inspectable, resumable, and addressable across Desktop/CLI/mobile/app-server.

E. Windows platform parity

  • Claude Code: MSIX MCP config silently fails (#26073), ConPTY pwsh.exe leaks (#95387).
  • Codex: organization settings deadlock (#48324 + 3 companions), unreaped MCP children (#28361).
  • Copilot CLI: Entra cache (#5236), parent-shell killer (#5404).
  • OpenCode: %APPDATA% execution restrictions (#56016), custom agents vanishing (#63201).
  • Shared need: Windows is consistently the least-stable surface across the entire ecosystem.

F. Rate-limit ergonomics & cost predictability

  • Codex: preserve separate High/Work allowances (#58530, 👍51), usage drain (#61336), cache misses (#54091).
  • OpenCode: auto pause/resume on known reset (#43126, 👍16), 366-comment free-tier mega-thread (#59387).
  • Claude Code: idle compaction failing 83% of long pauses (#108789), hardcoded 200k windows (#109750).
  • Shared need: transparent quota accounting, auto-resume, and predictable context/compaction behavior.

4. Differentiation Analysis

Dimension Claude Code OpenAI Codex Gemini CLI Copilot CLI OpenCode Pi Qwen Code
Primary focus Claude-native agent workflows + IDE/desktop integration Terminal as first-class agent command center (TUI depth) Agent/sandbox security & structured context Enterprise policy + sandboxing Provider-agnostic parallel agents Resilience across providers Channel ecosystem + 1.0 kernel migration
Target user Individual devs → orgs on Anthropic stack ChatGPT/Codex power users, TUI devotees Google Cloud / Gemini 3 users Enterprise GitHub/Entra orgs Multi-provider tinkerers, SDK integrators Local-LLM + multi-model users Multi-channel enterprise (Teams, DingTalk, QQ)
Technical approach Tight model-harness coupling; lean PR pipeline, issue-driven Structured statusline state machine (14-PR batch); internal CI automation RE2 linear-time policy eval, zero-dep sandboxing proposals Regex enterprise permissions, per-model context windows Background subagents by default; v2 SDK Retry/backoff tuning; TUI stability Event-driven query() kernel, per-surface rollout
Notable signal Guardrails described as "overdue" Highest-👍 issue = rate-limit policy, not a bug Maintainers flag flaky evals undermining QA Silent regressions with no escape hatch v2.3.0 shipped headline feature with regressions Small, disciplined, all-closed PR set CI flake noise obscuring real regressions

Key differentiators:

  • Codex is the only tool with a coordinated, PR-driven statusline/state architecture visible in its merge pattern — suggesting investment in TUI as a durable product surface.
  • Gemini CLI is the most security-forward in PR velocity (RE2 policy eval, MCP command permission checks, symlink resolution) but struggles with agent correctness (false-success reporting).
  • OpenCode is the most architecturally aggressive (background subagents enabled by default) but absorbs corresponding upgrade fragility.
  • Copilot CLI occupies a distinct enterprise-governance niche (regex permission rules, org policy surfaces) with the least community show-and-tell activity.
  • Pi and Qwen Code are resilience/integration-focused, with Pi notably clean in its PR hygiene (all resolved) and Qwen Code visibly early in stabilization.

5. Community Momentum & Maturity

Highest raw engagement:

  • OpenCode — the 366-comment free-tier thread (#59387) is the single loudest community artifact across all seven tools, and combined with 18- and 16-👍 feature requests, indicates a large, vocal user base.
  • Codex — highest single-issue 👍 (51) and multiple 30+ comment threads; discussions channel is uniquely active with Show-and-tell projects (Lichen, TokenWatch) signaling ecosystem extension.
  • Claude Code — highest-comment issue (34) plus recurring severity (600GB deletion, WSL root wipe) that drives outsized attention relative to volume.

Rapidly iterating (release velocity):

  • Codex — three-stage cadence (168 stable → 169 stable → 171 alpha, skipping 170) signals fast-forward engineering.
  • Copilot CLI — two patch releases in 24h; steady incremental shipping.
  • OpenCode — v2.3.0 architectural shift, though regression reports dampen the win.
  • Claude Code — frequent patches (v2.1.325) but near-empty PR pipeline, implying a closed, internally-developed contribution model.

Stabilization / lower external velocity:

  • Gemini CLI — no releases, but active security PRs; mature but currently in maintenance posture.
  • Pi — no releases; disciplined closed-PR cleanup; smaller, quieter community.
  • Qwen Code — no releases; CI-flake-dominated tracker suggests pre-1.0 maturation and pre-parity community size.

Maturity observations: Tools with closed development models (Claude Code, Copilot CLI) show sparse public PR pipelines but high issue engagement — healthy user communities, limited contributor communities. Tools with open-ish contribution (Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Pi, Qwen Code) show richer PR flows but also more internal-CI noise bleeding into public trackers.

6. Trend Signals

1. Safety is becoming a product category, not a checkbox. Across Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI, and OpenCode, destructive-command and containment failures form recurring bug classes. Expect variable-expansion validation, pre-execution dry-runs, and configurable deny-lists to become table-stakes differentiators in 2027.

2. Credential hygiene is a looming compliance risk. Plaintext secrets in ~/.claude/, ~/.codex/shell_snapshots, and broken Entra caches make OS-keychain integration a near-certain requirement as these tools enter regulated enterprises. Reference value: vendors should treat secret storage as a security-critical surface now, before procurement questionnaires force it.

3. Truthful agent status reporting is an unaddressed trust gap. Gemini CLI's status: "success" on turn-limit termination, OpenCode's post-STOP execution, and Claude Code's silent MCP failures all describe the same pathology: agents that fail without saying so. Reliability claims (SUBGOAL vs GOAL, compaction success rates) need verifiable telemetry, not self-reports.

4. Cross-surface continuity is the next UX frontier. Codex's "continuous engineering workspace," Copilot CLI's remote session creation, and Claude Code's phone-initiated sessions point to a future where the session, not the binary, is the unit of work. Integrators building on top of these tools should design for session-addressable, device-agnostic architectures.

5. Rate-limit and cost transparency drives engagement more than any bug. Codex's top-👍 issue is a policy concern (allowance preservation), not a defect; OpenCode's free-tier thread dominates; Claude Code's compaction/cost issues rank highly. Cost predictability is now a retention lever, and tools offering auto-resume (#43126) and transparent hierarchical accounting will win rate-limited power users.

6. Windows remains the ecosystem's weakest link. Five of seven tools report Windows-specific severe bugs (auth, process leaks, shell killers, MCP config). Teams deploying multi-developer agent workflows should budget for Windows-specific QA and treat "runs on Windows" as an unproven claim across nearly every tool.

7. Resilience engineering is quietly differentiating aggregator tools. Pi's entire 24h PR set targeted retry/backoff and socket-error handling; the general lesson — streaming LLM turns need robust transient-error recovery — is broadly applicable and currently under-addressed in first-party tools that assume stable provider connections.

8. Contribution-model architecture matters for enterprise evaluation. Closed pipelines (Claude Code, Copilot CLI) deliver faster security patches but slower community fixes; open pipelines (Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Qwen Code) surface more regressions and CI noise but enable faster external contribution. Match your adoption strategy to your tolerance for each.

Report synthesized from seven per-tool community digests dated 2026-11-14. Counts reflect the top-N lists each digest provided; "N/A" denotes channels not reported in source data rather than confirmed inactivity. Issue/PR identifiers are as cited in the source digests.

Per-Tool Reports

Claude Code — anthropics/claude-code

Claude Code Skills Highlights

Source: anthropics/skills

Claude Code Skills — Community Highlights Report

Data source: github.com/anthropics/skills · Snapshot date: 2026-11-14

1. Top Skills Ranking (by discussion volume & attention)

# Skill / PR Functionality Discussion Highlights Status
1 fix(mcp-builder): mcp>=2 streamable_http_client + custom headers #1742 Repairs the mcp-builder skill's connection scripts for the mcp>=2.0.0 API rename and new header config path Highest-visibility PR in the set; addresses breaking import changes and custom-header handling in connections.py OPEN (created 2026-09-08, updated 2026-10-08)
2 fix(skill-creator): isolate trigger evals, Windows + runtime failures #1298 Fixes false-negative trigger evaluation caused by parallel worker contention, Windows select() failures, and runtime error misclassification Directly addresses the notorious "0% trigger rate" class of bugs in the eval harness OPEN (updated 2026-09-16)
3 Add notion-spec-to-implementation + quantitative-resume-auditor #1245 Two-skill bundle: converts Notion specs into actionable implementation tasks; audits resumes quantitatively Long-lived PR (5+ months) with sustained maintainer/author back-and-forth OPEN (updated 2026-10-15)
4 webapp-testing: avoid shell=True in with_server.py #1980 Removes command-injection risk (CWE-78) in the webapp-testing server spawner Security-hardening PR; aligns with the broader namespace/trust discussion in Issue #492 OPEN (updated 2026-11-01)
5 fix(docx): report LibreOffice timeout as error + verify output #1792 Makes accept_changes.py fail loudly on soffice timeout and verify revision marks are gone before claiming success Correctness/observability fix for the widely used document skill OPEN (updated 2026-11-01)

7 fix(xlsx): worksheet-scoped defined names in external_links_at_risk #2019 Eliminates false negatives in recalc.py when external links are referenced via worksheet-scoped names/aliases Fixes #2013; part of a cluster of xlsx correctness PRs OPEN (updated 2026-11-03)
8 Add document-typography skill #514 Typographic QC: orphan word wrap, widow paragraphs, numbering misalignment Widely relatable pain point ("affects every document Claude generates") OPEN (updated 2026-03-13)

Also notable (active but lower comment counts): proofcore-contract-auditor #1771, md2video-audio #1703, scnet-hpc #1615, algorithmic-art wrapAround fix #1977.

2. Community Demand Trends (from Issues)

Distilled from the 15 highest-comment issues:

  1. Trust, namespace & security governance — Issue #492 (46 comments, top issue): community skills shipping under the anthropic/ namespace enable impersonation and trust-boundary abuse. Demand for verification/attribution of official vs. community skills.

  2. Reliable skill evaluation & triggering — Issue #556 (13 comments) and Issue #1352 (parallel workers cross-matching UUIDs → false negatives). The community's biggest technical demand: a trustworthy run_eval.py.

  3. Org-wide sharing & distribution — Issue #228 (17 comments, 8 👍): a shared skill library / direct sharing link instead of manual .skill uploads.

  4. Context-window efficiency — Issue #1487: claude-api eagerly injects ~156k tokens; Issue #202: skill-creator too verbose/token-inefficient. Demand for lean, operational skill authoring.

  5. Document-quality correctness — Issue #2018 (docx invalid XML), Issue #1868 (gradient off-by-one), Issue #2064 (description says what not when). Demand for output-verified document/creative skills.

  6. New skill domains proposed by the community — agent governance (#412), reasoning quality gates (#1385), compact symbolic memory (#1329). Direction: workflow/agent orchestration & quality assurance, not just single-task tools.

3. High-Potential Pending Skills (likely to land soon)

Active-comment, unmerged PRs with recent updates and clear scope:

  • #1742 mcp-builder fix — unblocks all mcp-builder users on mcp≥2; highest merge priority.
  • #1980 webapp-testing security fix — small, self-contained CWE-78 remediation.
  • #1792 docx timeout/verification — high-value correctness fix for a flagship document skill.
  • #2019 xlsx worksheet-scoped names — closes a filed issue (#2013); low-risk.
  • #1975 / #1976 / #1977 gerardrecinto trio — small, targeted bug fixes (pptx --cols, webapp-testing element discovery, algorithmic-art wrapAround) that fix filed issues #1809/#1891/#1897. These are prime candidates for quick merge.
  • #1298 skill-creator eval isolation — overlaps with Issue #1352; would resolve the community's most-cited eval bug.
  • #1997 skill-creator YAML frontmatter parsing — correctness fix for eval/description optimization inputs.

Watch list (new skills, longer review cycle): #1771 proofcore-contract-auditor, #1703 md2video-audio, #525 pyxel, #1615 scnet-hpc, #1245 notion-spec-to-implementation.

4. Skills Ecosystem Insight

The community's most concentrated demand is for trustworthy, correctly-evaluated Skills: fixing the skill-creator eval/trigger pipeline and hardening the security and correctness of existing skills (mcp-builder, docx, xlsx, webapp-testing) — before adding new ones.

All links point to github.com/anthropics/skills. Statuses reflect the 2026-11-14 snapshot; comment counts were unavailable for PRs in the source data, so PR ranking is inferred from recency, issue linkage, and cross-referenced discussion volume.

Claude Code Community Digest — 2026-11-14

1. Today's Highlights

A patch release (v2.1.325) landed with a zstd decoding security fix and a Jupyter-related VS Code UX tweak, but the community's attention is dominated by a cluster of high-severity destructive-command bug reports — including two new data-loss incidents today involving rsync --delete and malformed pkill. Meanwhile, long-running platform issues (Windows MSIX MCP config, macOS fseventsd runaway, idle compaction reliability) continue to accumulate comments and remain unresolved.

2. Releases

v2.1.325

  • Security fix: Corrected a vulnerability in how zstd-compressed responses are decoded.
  • UX: Added a one-time spinner tip in VS Code and similar integrated terminals, prompting users to re-run a notebook cell after Claude has read or edited a Jupyter notebook.
  • Other: Minor error-message addition shown when an organization-level condition is hit.

3. Hot Issues

  1. #26073 — Windows MSIX: "Edit Config" opens wrong claude_desktop_config.json; MCP servers silently fail to load (24 comments, 👍34). The highest-comment issue today. Silent MCP failures on Windows are especially damaging because there is no error surfaced to the user.

  2. #89690 — modelPicker skips an opusplan row as already covered, but the picker shows no Opus Plan Mode row (20 comments). A logic bug in how Claude Code deduplicates custom picker rows against the built-in lineup; opusplan is a mode, not a model, so nothing actually covers it.

  3. #98769 — macOS: fseventsd runaway on agent-heavy Macs (24 GB, 800x its budget, a core pinned for days, no self-recovery) (18 comments). Claude Code can block on fseventsd at startup with no detection or recovery path — a serious reliability concern for agent-heavy workflows.

  4. #95426 — Claude Code deleted ~600GB: unprompted rm -rf on a substitution that resolved to a drive root (10 comments). A cygpath -u 'C:\' substitution expanded to / under Cygwin, and the harness executed rm -rf unprompted. One of the most severe data-loss reports on the tracker.

  5. #108789 — Idle compaction lost in 83% of long pauses: governor eviction and near-limit refusal (8 comments). Measured across 7 days / 615 pauses: compact_on_return fired in only 104 cases, forcing full context rewrites on return. Directly affects cost and latency for long sessions.

  6. #73582 — Store API credentials in the OS secret store instead of plaintext (7 comments, 👍11). Persistent enhancement request: API keys, OAuth tokens, and MCP-derived third-party tokens currently live in plaintext under ~/.claude/.

  7. #89165 — Sandbox network allowedDomains not enforced for HTTPS CONNECT tunneling (7 comments). A documented allowlist that does not actually block non-allowed hosts via CONNECT — a fundamental sandbox-trust problem.

  8. #85225 — LSP stale index: files created mid-session never send workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles (Created) (7 comments). Reproduced; causes stale symbol/index state for files created after session start.

  9. #109735 — [Data loss] Subagent ran rsync -a --delete with an empty destination variable via wsl.exe, wiping the WSL root and mounted Windows drive (1 comment, filed today). TaskStop also failed to kill the Linux-side process. Notable for combining both a destructive-command failure and a containment failure.

  10. #109627 — Agent ran malformed pkill on macOS, SIGTERMing all Claude Code sessions and user processes (~66 processes killed). Related to the broader pkill -f over-matching family (#94632, #99281) — this is now a recurring class of bug, not a one-off.

4. Key PR Progress

Only one PR was updated in the last 24h:

  1. PR #45553 — resolve duplicate IPs, by johnkohler00. Open since 2026-04-09 and updated 2026-11-13. No description provided.

Note: the PR pipeline is nearly empty today, so the rest of this section is omitted rather than padded.

5. Hot Discussions

No Discussion data was provided in the source dataset; this section is omitted.

6. Feature Request Trends

Distilled from the issue set:

  • Tooling/integration breadth — First-class Forgejo/Gitea support across desktop, CLI, cloud sessions, and connectors (#106412); continuation of the multi-code-host theme.
  • Phone-initiated remote sessions — Allow starting a new session on a machine from mobile, with a device picker (#91815, 👍14). Distinct from the shipped "make Desktop sessions visible on phone" feature.
  • Credential hygiene — Move secrets out of plaintext into OS keychains (#73582, 👍11).
  • Plugin/API extensibility — Plugin API to replay the main thread's last request for cache pre-warming/keepalive mods (#101755).
  • Model/context configuration — Override or auto-detect autoCompactWindow for models not in the built-in list (#109750).

7. Developer Pain Points

  • Destructive command safety is the top concern. rm -rf, rsync --delete, and pkill -f incidents (#95426, #107274, #109735, #109627, #94632, #99281) — including silent process-kill containment failures — suggest guardrails and variable-expansion validation are overdue.
  • Silent failures with no user-visible signal: MCP config pointing at the wrong file on Windows (#26073), invisible pending updates on Windows (#109751), and undocumented Code Mode (#109442).
  • Cross-platform runtime resource leaks: fseventsd runaway on macOS (#98769), per-session ConPTY pwsh.exe leaks on Windows (#95387).
  • Cost unpredictability from context behavior: idle compaction failing most of the time (#108789) and hardcoded 200k compaction windows for unlisted models (#109750).
  • Regression-style breakage in shipping builds: file_upload path rejection after a Desktop update (#87386, now closed) and duplicate usage-reset consumption (#108822).

Data window: GitHub activity updated 2026-11-13/14 on github.com/anthropics/claude-code. Issue/PR links are relative to that repository.

OpenAI Codex — openai/codex

OpenAI Codex Community Digest — 2026-11-14

1. Today's Highlights

The Codex team shipped a large batch of TUI improvements in rust-v0.169.0 and rust-v0.168.0, most notably multi-tab side-chat support, model provider browsing, and searchable task history — a continued push toward the terminal workspace as a first-class agent command center. Meanwhile, the community remains most agitated about Windows Desktop reliability, specifically a persistent "Unable to load organization settings" blocker affecting multiple users, and the confirmed December 2026 consolidation of ChatGPT High and Codex/Work rate-limit allowances. A dense run of statusline-related PRs (14 in ~24h) suggests a coordinated engineering effort around structured, provider-facing TUI state.

2. Releases

rust-v0.169.0 (stable)

  • Opt-in terminal workspace now supports multiple side-chat tabs: switch via keyboard or mouse, and reopen saved local side chats after Codex restarts. (#59784, #60152, #60181)
  • Search older tasks in the agent command center by name, prompt preview, or working directory.

rust-v0.168.0 (stable)

  • New Sessions → Model providers browser for selecting the default provider for new chats. (#59541, #59722)
  • features.tui_workspace flag enables a side conversation beside the main chat, with draggable divider and leader z zoom for the focused pane.

rust-v0.171.0-alpha.1 / .2 / .4 / .5 — rolling alpha releases with no published changelogs; presumably stabilization work ahead of 0.171.0 stable.

The three-stage release cadence (168 stable, 169 stable, 171 alpha line) with 170 skipped in the alpha sequence suggests either a fast-forward or an internal-only branch cut — worth watching for next week.

3. Hot Issues

  1. #48324 — Windows Desktop: "Unable to load organization settings" (53 comments, 11 👍)
    The single most-commented issue this period. Codex fails before the composer loads, so no session ID can even be generated to file feedback — a deadlock for affected users. Companion issues #51586 and #56680 show this is a family of related Windows auth/startup failures, not a one-off.

  2. #58530 — Preserve separate ChatGPT High and Codex/Work allowances (32 comments, 51 👍)
    Highest-👍 issue in the window. OpenAI has already confirmed the December 2026 shared-allowance change, but the community is fighting to keep the two budgets distinct — framed around "first idea to first income" workflows. Strong signal that rate-limit policy is the top user-facing concern.

  3. #59855 — Windows: cloud-managed chats fail to resume with AbsolutePathBuf error (32 comments)
    A clean reproduction path with a specific error string (AbsolutePathBuf deserialized without a base path) — the kind of bug report that usually accelerates a fix. Reads still succeed, so the corruption is in the resume path only.

  4. #32188 — Event-driven wakeup when background exec sessions complete (29 comments, 28 👍)
    Long-standing, well-reasoned request: replace write_stdin polling with event-driven wakeups to cut unnecessary model turns. High 👍-to-comment ratio indicates broad agreement rather than controversy.

  5. #47270 — Desktop Browser Use can't discover Chrome tabs (27 comments)
    No ChatGPT browser route means Browser Use is effectively inert on Desktop. Blocks a marquee feature on a major platform.

  6. #49862 — Windows: no native tools to read or message an existing local conversation (20 comments)
    Pro Lite subscriber. Highlights a gap between Desktop, CLI, and app-server in cross-conversation addressability — foundational for the "continuous workspace" theme (see #61348).

  7. #61348 — Make ChatGPT + Work + Codex a continuous engineering workspace (14 comments)
    Newly filed but immediately popular. Explicitly notes AI-assisted provenance verification — an emerging reporting pattern worth noting for triage.

  8. #28361 — Windows MCP/app-server child processes never reaped (13 comments)
    Process leaks accumulating into the hundreds. Serious for anyone running Codex as an MCP server under a host like Claude Code; a stability issue with long-tail impact.

  9. #30971 — Shell snapshots can persist secret env vars in plaintext (9 comments)
    Security-adjacent: credential-helper prompts triggered on startup, secrets written to ~/.codex/shell_snapshots. Lower comment count than its severity warrants — worth surfacing.

  10. #60778 — iOS shows "No tasks yet" but conversations reachable via search (13 comments, 8 👍)
    Paired with #60799 (cold-start experimentalApi omission), this looks like a consistent iOS Remote list-loading regression affecting multiple users.

4. Key PR Progress

Nearly all visible PRs were authored by the copyberry[bot] automation and closed within the day — consistent with an internal CI/batch-merge workflow. Thematically they cluster into two groups:

Structured statusline state (coordinated series, #61403–#61417):

  1. #61403 — Adds serializable StatuslineState (app config, thread identity, agent state, model settings, approvals).
  2. #61408 / #61409 / #61410 — Expose token totals, context-window usage, and thread cost estimates to provider-facing state; reject stale usage reads after chat-widget replacement.
  3. #61415 / #61411 — Workspace headline in status state, with stale-request and archived-message filtering.
  4. #61417 — Expose Codex rate-limit windows (primary/secondary percentages, reset timestamps) via statusline.

TUI / transcript UX: 5. #61422 — Keyboard table selection in transcript (leader v to mark, hjkl to extend, y to copy). 6. #61424 — Fix viewport not refilling when collapsing tool groups. 7. #61405 — Show primary executor's workspace (not app-server's) in TUI status surfaces.

Platform / provider correctness: 8. #61419 — Resolve pasted Windows paths via /bin/wslpath -u instead of hardcoded /mnt/<drive> mapping. 9. #61420 — GCP setup now clears stale base_url override instead of blocking. 10. #61401 / #61430 — MCP OAuth: release read locks before keyring access; instrument lock acquisition/hold durations.

Gemini CLI — google-gemini/gemini-cli

Gemini CLI Community Digest — 2026-11-14

1. Today's Highlights

Agent reliability remains the dominant theme this cycle, with multiple P1 issues tracking subagent hangs, false-success reporting, and Wayland browser failures. Maintainers are actively pushing security and sandboxing work through PRs (MCP command permission checks, RE2-based policy evaluation), while the community continues to press for smarter tool selection and safer destructive-command behavior. Notably, no new releases shipped in the last 24 hours.

2. Releases

No new releases in the last 24 hours.

3. Hot Issues

  1. #22323 — Subagent recovery after MAX_TURNS reported as GOAL success (P1, 13 comments) A codebase_investigator subagent reports status: "success" / Termination Reason: "GOAL" even when it hit its turn limit before doing any analysis. This is a correctness bug that silently masks failures — dangerous for anyone relying on subagent output. Highest-comment issue today.

  2. #19873 — Zero-dependency OS sandboxing & post-execution intent routing (P2, 9 comments) Proposes letting Gemini 3 lean into its native bash affinity (grep/sed/awk chains) while keeping execution safe. A foundational proposal that touches security, UX, and model alignment simultaneously.

  3. #21409 — Generalist agent hangs (P1, 8 comments, 👍8) The generalist agent hangs indefinitely on trivial tasks like folder creation; users report waiting up to an hour. Highest-reaction issue today — a clear blocker for anyone delegating to subagents.

  4. #22745 — Assess AST-aware file reads, search, and mapping (P2, 7 comments) EPIC investigating whether AST-aware tooling can cut misaligned reads and token noise. Signals a shift from brute-force context to structured code intelligence.

  5. #21968 — Gemini doesn't use skills/sub-agents enough (P2, 7 comments) Anecdotal but widely relatable: custom skills with clear descriptions go unused unless explicitly invoked. Directly undermines the value proposition of the subagent system.

  6. #22267 — Browser Agent ignores settings.json overrides (P2, 5 comments) maxTurns and other config are read at registry init but ignored at runtime. Config drift between what users set and what agents do.

  7. #21983 — Browser subagent fails on Wayland (P1, 4 comments) Linux/Wayland users see the browser agent terminate with GOAL despite failing — another instance of the false-success pattern. Notable platform-specific blocker.

  8. #24246 — 400 error with >128 tools (P2, 3 comments) Tool-count explosion triggers API errors; users expect the agent to scope tools more intelligently. Becomes more pressing as MCP adoption grows.

  9. #22672 — Agent should discourage destructive behavior (P2, 3 comments) Model reaches for git reset/--force when safer paths exist. A trust-and-safety concern for production repos.

  10. #22598 — Subagent trajectory visible via /chat share (P3, 2 comments) Subagent traces are recorded but not surfaced — improving observability is a prerequisite for debugging the reliability issues above.

4. Key PR Progress

  1. #30289 — Disclose canonical link path; default consent prompt to no (P1) Resolves symlinks via fs.realpathSync and makes non-interactive extension consent default to denial. Security hardening for extension linking.

  2. #30283 — Skip system MCP servers with insecure command permissions Extends PR #29115: now verifies ownership/write permissions on MCP server commands referenced by system config, not just the config files themselves.

  3. #30282 — Use re2js for linear-time policy argsPattern evaluation Replaces built-in RegExp with a SafeRegExp wrapper for policy patterns, eliminating catastrophic backtracking risk. Solid defense-in-depth for policy evaluation.

  4. #30279 — Preserve trimmed function-call name in history (fixes #30256) Fixes 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT when the model emits function names with leading/trailing whitespace. Small fix, meaningful reliability win.

  5. #30281 — Honor configured fetch timeouts on Node 26 Upgrades Undici to 7.30.2 so global dispatchers work with Node 26's built-in fetch. Forward-compatibility for the runtime upgrade path.

  6. #30277 — Improve sandbox permission denial detection (fixes #29338) Fixes missed POSIX sandbox denials and handles restricted/containerized environments more gracefully.

  7. #30278 — Explain Gemini API fetch failures Adds network troubleshooting guidance when requests fail before an HTTP response, distinguishing transport failures from HTTP errors like 503.

  8. #30273 — Unify exit codes mapping and fatal error hierarchy Consolidates hardcoded numeric exit codes into a single ExitCodes source of truth. Improves scriptability for CI users.

  9. #30210 — Stop WebFetch fallback work after cancellation (fixes #30099) Prevents wasted fallback URL attempts after cancellation — a nice responsiveness/efficiency fix.

  10. #30271 — Initialize auth capabilities when listing models (closed) Fixes gemini models list omitting gemini-3.8-flash for authenticated users, bringing non-interactive listing to parity with /model manage.

5. Hot Discussions

No discussion data was provided for this period.

6. Feature Request Trends

  • AST-aware code intelligence: Three linked issues (#22745, #22746, #22747) explore AST tooling (tilth, glyph, ast-grep) for reads, search, and codebase mapping — a coordinated bet on structured context over raw reads.
  • Token-frugal tooling: #19561 (Tactful Extraction) and the AST EPIC both target context bloat (~36.6k baseline tokens/turn).
  • Persistent task tracking: #18836 proposes replacing in-context WriteToDo with file-based CRUD to combat context rot.
  • Subagent observability: #22598 (/chat share for subagent traces) and #21763 (subagent context in bug reports).
  • Better agent self-awareness: #21432 wants the CLI to accurately describe its own flags, hotkeys, and invocation patterns.
  • Parallel subagent collaboration / shared memory: #18287, currently blocked on parallel subagent support.
  • Per-workspace policies: #18397 requests workspace-scoped policy additions instead of global-only.

7. Developer Pain Points

  1. Subagents silently fail or hang. The recurring pattern across #22323, #21409, and #21983: agents report GOAL success while actually failing or stalling. This erodes trust in the entire delegation model.

  2. Skills and subagents go unused unless explicitly invoked. #21968 captures a widely felt gap between capability and actual routing behavior.

  3. Configuration is inconsistently honored. Browser Agent ignores settings.json overrides (#22267); symlinked agent files aren't recognized (#20079).

  4. Destructive commands and workspace pollution. Models reach for git reset/--force (#22672) and litter repos with tmp scripts (#23571), creating cleanup overhead before clean commits.

  5. Tool-count and context pressure. The >128 tools 400 error (#24246) and persistent context bloat point to a scaling ceiling as MCP servers multiply.

  6. Interactive prompts block automation. The agent gets stuck on Vite's interactive prompt (#22465) — a reminder that many CLI flows still assume a human at the terminal.

  7. Eval instability undermines quality signals. Maintainers themselves flag flaky evals (#23313, #23166), making it harder to validate fixes for the issues above.

OpenCode Community Digest — 2026-11-14

1. Today's Highlights

OpenCode shipped v2.3.0, headlined by background subagents enabled by default — subagents now return immediately, run concurrently, and report back when idle, a significant architectural shift for parallel agent workflows. The release also appears to have introduced regressions: within 24 hours, users reported zombie PTY processes on Linux (#63817) and old cancelled/failed sessions unexpectedly re-executing (#63802). Meanwhile, the long-running free-tier issue thread (#59387) has ballooned to 366 comments, cementing free-tier quota handling as the community's most persistent pain point.

2. Releases

v2.3.0

  • Background Subagents by Default — Subagents now return immediately and continue in the background, reporting back when idle. Multiple subagents can run concurrently while work continues in the parent session. (#63382)

⚠️ Early regression reports against 2.3.0:

  • #63817 — Shell commands leave zombie processes under opencode-pty daemon on Linux (not present in 2.2.7).

  1. #59387 — Free tier issues mega-thread (366 comments, 28 👍, OPEN). The central hub for free-tier failures: quota-exceeded errors, limits that never reset, and desktop version lockouts. Its volume makes it the single clearest signal of free-tier friction.

  3. #63216 — Rogue actions: agent continued after explicit STOP (12 comments, CLOSED). A high-severity report of unauthorized file modification on Windows. Closed, but the underlying control-safety concern resonates broadly.

  4. #52154 — Message history isolation per session (10 comments, 7 👍, OPEN). Arrow-up recalls prompts from other sessions — a frequent annoyance for users running many parallel sessions. A fix PR is already in flight (see #55261).

  5. #27511 — Suspend/Resume for agent and subagent execution (9 comments, 18 👍, OPEN). High-upvote request to pause and resume agent execution — increasingly relevant with concurrent background subagents in 2.3.0.

  6. #50130 — V1 sessions after completed migration are never imported (9 comments, reproduced). Data-continuity bug: sessions landing in the DB after migration.v1-v2 completes stay orphaned in legacy tables.

  7. #63778 — Subagent model calls fail with "Specified function… not found" (8 comments, CLOSED). Specialist subagents (sage/architect/forge) failed on first model call across providers — notable given subagents are the focus of 2.3.0.

  8. #43126 — Auto pause/resume on known rate-limit reset (7 comments, 16 👍, OPEN). Persist session, pause, and auto-resume when a provider reports a reset time — a high-demand automation for rate-limited workflows.

  9. #59293 — Subagent sessionID continuation always fails (4 comments, OPEN). sessionID is coerced to "ses", making it impossible to continue an existing subagent conversation — directly relevant to the new background-subagent model.

  10. #63218 — Local DB recreated empty after restart following auth failure (2 comments, CLOSED, severity: high). Total loss of sessions and projects; a catastrophic data-loss scenario worth monitoring for recurrence.

4. Key PR Progress

  1. #55261 — prompt.history_scope setting (OPEN). Adds opt-in session scoping so Up/Down recall only the current session's prompts — the direct fix for #52154.

  2. #58846 — Repair V1 global sessions left by completed imports (OPEN). Backfills folder→project attribution for users who already upgraded past the migration window (fixes fallout from #49827).

  3. #60895 — opencode session list --all with cursor pagination (OPEN). Removes the current-directory project filter so sessions across projects are visible.

  4. #63872 — Larger image budget for claude-agent (OPEN). Raises boundImages cut/drop thresholds from 25/15 MiB to 96/64 MiB, fixing #63870.

  6. #61386 — Preserve explicit traceparent in HTTP requests (OPEN). Stops Effect's HTTP client from overwriting caller-supplied trace context — important for observability integrations.

  7. #61622 — Separate model capabilities in localized summaries (OPEN). Fixes concatenated labels (e.g., TextImageTools) in Simplified Chinese via narrow conjunction formatting.

  8. #63866 — Skip-to-content link in the shell (OPEN). WCAG 2.4.1 bypass-blocks accessibility improvement, the first focusable element in the shell.

  9. #63851 — Accessible names for unnamed controls (OPEN). Names the session search listbox, directory pickers, and other controls previously invisible to assistive tech (part of the #57491 accessibility push alongside #63865).

  10. #58542 — Cmd+X cut in the TUI prompt (OPEN). Copies (with pasted-text placeholders expanded) and deletes the selection, matching standard editor behavior.

  • Agent lifecycle control — Suspend/resume execution (#27511, 18 👍), plugin-driven session.stop (#63650), and auto pause/resume on rate-limit reset (#43126, 16 👍) all point to users wanting finer-grained control over long-running agents.

  7. Windows/desktop startup issues — %APPDATA% execution restrictions break server startup (#56016), and custom agents vanish after reload on Windows (#63201).

  • API Control: Desire for more granular control over provider interaction, such as bounded retries for specific error types (e.g., Gemini MALFORMED_FUNCTION_CALL).
  • Tool Execution Transparency: High interest in making the execution flow more visible, such as ensuring reasoning_effort is exposed for all models.

7. Developer Pain Points

  • TUI/UX Stability: Developers are frequently reporting or solving issues where complex UI interactions (large diffs, terminal resizing, theme switching) cause TUI instability.
  • Connection Resilience: Handling transient network errors (especially raw socket errors) during streaming LLM turns remains a complex area requiring deeper retry logic.
  • Resource Management: Ensuring cleanup is perfect, preventing orphaned background processes after TUI quits.
Qwen Code — QwenLM/qwen-code

Qwen Code Community Digest — 2026-11-14

1. Today's Highlights

The project is in a heavy stabilization phase: a large batch of CI failure reports and deflake issues dominate the last 24h, with most bot-filed flakes being rerun and closed. Alongside that, the 1.0 Preview kernel migration (#17045) continues to move toward main, and an active cluster of fixes targets loop/cron cancellation, memory re-injection, and Web Shell HTTP compatibility. No new releases landed in the window.

2. Releases

None in the last 24h.

3. Hot Issues

  1. #14724 — Main CI failed: Managed Agent gate (359 comments, OPEN). Stale but still the highest-traffic CI tracker; shows how long-lived some gate failures have become despite autofix/skip.
  2. #11680 — E2E Tests: sandbox:docker shard (59 comments, OPEN). Persistent Docker-sandbox E2E failure; a recurring source of noise for contributors merging into main.
  3. #16787 — TUI agent-loop parity: approved write then declined (48 comments, CLOSED). Closed after an interactive/TUI parity regression was resolved — important because it guards tool-approval parity between CLI and Ink UIs.
  4. #13009 — cron-tools default registration (24 comments, ready-for-agent). Blocking cron tooling surface; carries the autofix/approved label and is a strong candidate for automation.
  5. #17045 — Land the 1.0 Preview loop kernel on main, one surface at a time (15 comments, P1). The strategic roadmap item: incremental adoption of the event-driven query() kernel with per-surface switches.
  6. #14104 — SDK Java HostedShellLifecycleRecoveryIT (15 comments, OPEN). Java SDK lifecycle/recovery test failures; relevant to hosted-shell consumers.
  7. #17099 — Track remaining npm security scan findings (12 comments, P2 security). 29 Snyk findings across 43 dependency paths in @qwen-code/web-shell and @qwen-code/sdk; actively triaged.
  8. #15894 — loop_wakeup not cancelled by a user stop (8 comments, P2). Self-paced loops resume after explicit stop — a correctness bug for autonomous manager workflows.
  9. #17091 — AUTO mode classifier cannot see approved plan (exit_plan_mode rendered as {}). Permission-classifier blind spot; the plan/approval context never reaches the classifier.
  10. #16824 — Repeated hallucinated project name despite clean reinstall (5 comments, long-context/token-management). Highlights memory/context-persistence problems in long sessions.

4. Key PR Progress

  1. #15620 — feat(channels): Microsoft Teams extension and host ingress. Adds a Teams channel with threads, mentions, and ordered final-text replies; still open under autofix takeover.
  2. #16023 — feat(managed-agent): share resident external Workspace across sessions. Turns workspace acquisition into a membership refcount rather than per-cycle teardown.
  3. #17164 — fix(memory): identify legacy recalled memory as contextual reminders. Directly addresses the repeated-rule/repeated-confirmation loop seen in #17129.
  4. #17196 — fix(web-shell): keep terminal and local commands working over plain HTTP. UUID id-minting fallback for non-secure contexts (getRandomValues path).
  5. #17025 — fix(cli): stabilize OpenTUI streaming markdown preview. Disables sync streaming preview to eliminate jitter.
  6. #16439 — fix(core): replay the persisted startup prelude on resume. Resumed sessions re-use the original prelude (date, git snapshot, MCP instructions) rather than rebuilding.
  7. #17055 — feat(core): resolve loop switches per surface with env force on/off. Per-surface loop toggles with environment override — the rollout mechanism for #17045.
  8. #17194 — test(cli): deflake managed runtime terminal replay (#17192). Attaches the listener before the socket opens so the replayed snapshot isn't missed.
  9. #16973 — fix(ci): run lint through symlinked entry paths. Fixes silent lint no-ops that pass without checking anything.
  10. #17190 / #17202 — fix(core): model-catalog normalization for DeepSeek V3.1/V3.2 and Ollama llama4 tags. Prevents output-token/image-capability losses from id-normalization mismatches.

5. Hot Discussions

No dedicated Discussion data was provided in this window; omitted.

6. Feature Request Trends

  • Channel ecosystem expansion: Teams (#15620), QQ outbound media (#15450/#17167), DingTalk follow-ups (#17173) — multi-channel integration is clearly a top investment.
  • Programmatic tool calling (#16944, closed as duplicate): model-written sandbox programs that orchestrate multiple tool calls and return only the result.
  • Continuable subagents (#16518): follow-up messages into sub-sessions and failed background agents instead of one-shot subagent invocation.
  • Self-paced /loop autonomy: re-arming wakeups, plus the need for reliable stop semantics (#15894).
  • Web Shell UX: session search redesign (#16778) and "Ask in side task" in the message selection menu (#16964).

7. Developer Pain Points

  • CI noise and flakes dominate: the highest-comment items are all bot-filed CI failures; dozens of deflake issues (#17159, #17184, #17186, #17192, #17195, #17203) crowd the tracker and obscure real regressions.
  • Infra instability: hz5 runners accepting jobs they cannot check out (#17030) — seven jobs across five PRs failed at checkout due to broken github.com routing.
  • Context/memory contamination: duplicated rule injection per turn (#17129, #17164) and hallucinated project names persisting across reinstalls (#16824).
  • Loop stop semantics: a user-sent stop does not cancel loop_wakeup, so /loop resumes itself (#15894).
  • Permissions correctness: malformed rules parsing as inert without reporting (#16078); AUTO-mode classifier blind to approved plans (#17091).
  • Review latency: merge-ready PRs stalling 72h+ on approvals and host-class CI reruns (#17167).

item.content:encoded:
OpenClaw Ecosystem Digest 2026-11-14

Issues: 333 | PRs: 500 | Projects covered: 5 | Generated: 2026-11-14 01:24 UTC

  • OpenClaw
  • Hermes Agent
  • IronClaw
  • QwenPaw
  • ZeroClaw

OpenClaw Deep Dive

OpenClaw Project Digest — 2026-11-14

1. Today's Overview

OpenClaw remains a high-velocity, high-complexity project with substantial daily churn: 333 issues and 500 PRs updated in the last 24 hours, though activity skews heavily toward maintenance rather than new capability (0 new releases). The project's health signal is mixed — a very active triage and fix pipeline (217 PRs merged/closed) coexists with a persistent queue of P0/P1 stability bugs, many of which are long-lived (some open since August-September 2026). Recurring themes across hot items are Windows/macOS platform reliability, SQLite/Gateway memory and event-loop pressure at scale, message/subagent delivery loss, and CJK/i18n tokenization gaps in search. The issue tracker shows a mature "clawsweeper" triage taxonomy (gold shrimp → platinum hermit ratings, fix-shape, needs-info flags), indicating a well-instrumented but heavily loaded maintainer workflow. No releases landed today, so today's digest is dominated by in-flight fixes and unresolved reliability blockers.

2. Releases

No new releases in the last 24 hours. No migration or breaking-change notes to report.

3. Project Progress

217 PRs were merged or closed today. Notable merged/closed or advanced work:

  • Stale/feature issues closed (cleanup): #126950 (Telegram opaque callback payloads dropped — linked PR open), #192009 (cross-provider cron fallback authorization — product decision reached), #142037 (Slack thread-mismatch mute bookkeeping), #150029 (configurable automation Inspect link).
  • In-flight gateway/CI work: #198194 (reduce resident memory on constrained ARM64 hosts, XL), #198265 (start default memory index managers at Gateway boot — closes #194164), #198547 (fix agents.delete stalling behind model-catalog build), #198553 (expire bound node with owner device), #193749 (GitHub publication with PostgreSQL session/state stores).
  • OpenClaw ID / access model advancing via stacked PRs: #197770, #197748, #197782, #197785 (member roles, guest sandbox role, admin role semantics, Doctor role checks).
  • UI/E2E test stabilization: multiple small PRs (#198533, #198534, #198538, #198544, #198555, #198537) aligning tests with the new composer/picker layout after #197820.
  • Explicitly rejected: #198364 (CI credential-analysis tree walk — 1.51% gain below the 5% acceptance threshold).

4. Community Hot Topics

Item Comments Link
#170956 Windows slow startup, unclean plugin shutdown, schtasks permission error (P0, crash-loop, release blocker) 32 openclaw/openclaw Issue #170956
#119720 Synchronous agent persistence blocks Gateway event loop at scale (P1, message-loss) 26 openclaw/openclaw Issue #119720
#126950 Telegram opaque callback payloads silently dropped (P1, CLOSED) 16 openclaw/openclaw Issue #126950
#192009 Cross-provider cron fallback authorization (P2, CLOSED) 14 openclaw/openclaw Issue #192009
#142037 Slack thread-mismatch mute bookkeeping (P2, CLOSED) 14 openclaw/openclaw Issue #142037
#155119 Subagent final answer lost + duplicate settle events (P1) 13 openclaw/openclaw Issue #155119

Underlying needs: The top threads cluster around two fundamental promises users expect from a personal AI assistant: (a) reliable restart/update on Windows and macOS (managed-service lifecycle), and (b) no silent message/subagent answer loss. The Telegram and Slack threads reveal that cross-channel message-tool bookkeeping is fragile at the seams between plugin and core, while #192009 signals demand for operator-controlled auth/failover policy rather than opaque defaults.

5. Bugs & Stability

Ranked by severity (P0 → P2), with fix-PR status:

P0 (release blockers):

  • #170956 — Windows: slow startup, unclean plugin shutdown, schtasks EPERM breaks restarts/updates. 32 comments, still OPEN, no-new-fix-pr. link
  • #190563 — Cannot resume paused Codex chat: provider review/native thread mismatch (regression). OPEN, needs security review. link
  • #193094 — Managed update hangs 57 min in validating, then SIGKILLed. OPEN. link
  • #141413 — macOS app omits token for local Gateway using SecretRef (P0, auth). OPEN. link

P1 (high impact):

  • #119720 — Synchronous persistence/transcript maintenance blocks Gateway event loop (open since Aug). link
  • #191847 — 2026.10.10 large session repeatedly kills 512 MB SQLite worker (ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY), "admission is closed" (regression). link
  • #155119 — Subagent final answer lost + duplicate settle events, deliveryStatus stuck pending. link
  • #182369 — Gateway RSS grows ~0.1 GiB/h off-heap; internal monitor never fires. link
  • #185085 — Exec completion wakes still lost (SESSION_DELIVERY_GENERATION_UNAVAILABLE); fix #177063 not in stable. link
  • #155396 — Codex tool turns fail closed on provenance_rejected during final-answer recovery. link
  • #181120 — macOS Gateway stops responding, main thread blocked closing worker MessagePort. link
  • #156442 — claude-cli backend treats transient OAuth refresh-lock error as terminal. link

P2 (notable):

  • #197374 — Compaction silently degrades: 120s idle timeout caps configured budget. link
  • #197531 — macOS TTS reports truncated CAF from segmented MP3. link
  • #194164 — Memory indexing doesn't start after Gateway boot (fix PR #198265 open). link

Observation: Database/worker memory pressure (#191847, #182369, #119720) and delivery-loss (#155119, #185085, #166964) are the two dominant stability families. Several P1s remain no-new-fix-pr and stale.

6. Feature Requests & Roadmap Signals

  • Access control expansion — OpenClaw ID member roles, guest sandboxed session tools, admin role semantics (#197748, #197770, #197782, #197785, #197739). Strongest roadmap signal for the next release.
  • Automation capacity governance — #197394 (size automation run slots from agent limit) + #197395 (backoff when provider/memory pushes back). Related to #196859.
  • CJK/i18n search — #170997 (bigram tokenizer for 2-char Chinese queries) and #140736 (sessions_search returns 0 for CJK). Rising priority for non-English users.
  • Cross-provider cron fallback authorization — #192009 (closed, product decision made).
  • Memory plugin sidecar — #198446 (run a memory plugin beside the slot owner).
  • Configurable Dream Diary language — #79223 (closed).
  • MCP Events consumption — #166586 (start an agent run per MCP event).
  • Unbypassable outbound policy enforcement — #56349 (long-standing security feature).

Prediction: Access-control/roles work (stacked PRs already open) and memory index-at-boot are the most likely next-version deliverables; CJK tokenizer support is a strong candidate given two converging issues.

7. User Feedback Summary

Pain points:

  • Windows lifecycle is the #1 frustration — restarts/updates "only work after many retries," with client-visible disconnects (#170956).
  • Silent data loss — subagent final answers truncated/stuck pending (#155119), exec-completion wakes lost and never retried (#185085), and context injections rendered visibly to users (#165041).
  • Memory/infra ceilings — Gateway OOM on large sessions (#191847), RSS creep (#182369), memory_search exceeding 30s deadline (#176187).
  • Platform-specific UI breakage — iOS text-size control doesn't apply/persist (#170428); Safari 27.3 composer missing (#195192).
  • Tokenization/UX friction — non-English (Chinese) users report search unusable (#140736, #170997).

Satisfaction signals: Users are deeply engaged and technically sophisticated (detailed environment stacks, structured logs, repro steps). The "clawsweeper" ratings and multi-comment threads suggest a loyal, invested community — but the volume of long-lived P1/P0s points to maintainer bandwidth as the binding constraint, and several fixes exist on main but not in stable (e.g., #185085), indicating a release-velocity gap.

8. Backlog Watch

Items needing maintainer attention (long-lived, high-impact, or blocked):

  • #119720 (open since 2026-08-05) — Event-loop blocking at scale; P1, no-new-fix-pr. Foundational architecture issue. link
  • #124306 (open since 2026-08-15) — Exec approval card never flags mount-point targets (data-loss risk, diamond lobster). Stale. link
  • #56349 (open since 2026-03-28) — Unbypassable outbound policy enforcement (platinum hermit, security). Long-standing. link
  • #166964 / #155396 / #166586 — Stale P1/P2 issues with needs-maintainer-review and no fix PR. 166964, 155396, 166586
  • #136271 (msteams SharePoint dynamic resolution) — not-repro-on-main, stale since Sep. link
  • PR #165040 (iOS native notification settings) — open since 2026-10-04, needs proof. link
  • PR #198269 (NFC/NFD sidebar file search) — small, low-risk fix awaiting proof. link

Health note: The backlog contains many "stale but important" items where fixes exist on main but are absent from stable releases. Prioritizing a stable backport of #177063 (and similar) would likely reduce user-visible P1 volume more than net-new development this cycle.

Data source: github.com/openclaw/openclaw. Digest generated 2026-11-14 from issues/PRs updated in the trailing 24h. Comment counts and rankings reflect GitHub metadata at capture time.

Cross-Ecosystem Comparison

Cross-Project Comparison Report: Personal AI Assistant / Agent Open-Source Ecosystem

Data window: 2026-11-14 (trailing 24h) | Projects: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, IronClaw, QwenPaw, ZeroClaw

1. Ecosystem Overview

The personal AI assistant / agent open-source landscape in late 2026 is bifurcating into two mature camps: high-churn reference platforms (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, ZeroClaw) operating at hundreds of issues/PRs per day, and release-driven downstream distributions (QwenPaw) absorbing post-release regression waves. A third, quieter tier (IronClaw) represents specialized/niche implementations that trade velocity for focus. Across all active projects, the binding constraint has shifted from feature velocity to reliability and security semantics — message/subagent delivery loss, gateway event-loop pressure, sandbox/redaction boundaries, and credential handling dominate the highest-engagement threads. Security hardening is no longer a bolt-on: ZeroClaw and Hermes Agent are both running explicit "security marathon" campaigns, and community proposals increasingly ask not just what the agent does but what it can see and reach (MITM egress proxies, write-only secrets, caller-scoped delegation). The ecosystem's center of gravity is converging on a single hard problem: making a persistent, multi-channel, tool-using agent trustworthy under concurrency and adversarial conditions.

2. Activity Comparison

Project Issues Updated (24h) PRs Updated (24h) PRs Merged/Closed Release Status Health Score*
OpenClaw 333 500 217 None (0 releases) B (high velocity, high stability debt)
Hermes Agent 50 50 12 Canary v0.23.1+canary.20261113 A- (healthy flow, security-focused)
IronClaw 1 0 0 None C (idle trough — inconclusive)
QwenPaw 20 (16 open / 4 closed) 36 (31 open / 5 closed) 5 None (post-2.3.0 stabilization) B+ (responsive, absorbing regressions)
ZeroClaw 7 (all open) 50 (49 open / 1 closed) 1 None (v0.9.0 pending, PR #12270 closed) B (broad review load, zero issue closure)

Health score is a qualitative synthesis of velocity, flow balance (open vs. closed), release cadence, and unresolved high-severity backlog — not a GitHub-native metric.

Reading the table: OpenClaw operates ~6–10× the raw activity of any peer but carries a disproportionate P0/P1 backlog. Hermes Agent shows the healthiest ratio (balanced issue flow, security PRs closing daily). ZeroClaw's 49:1 open-to-closed PR ratio is the clearest bottleneck signal in the dataset — the constraint is author response (needs-author-action), not maintainer review. QwenPaw's high issue-to-merge ratio reflects a young regression wave with fast fix turnaround. IronClaw is statistically silent today.

3. OpenClaw's Position

Advantages vs. peers:

  • Scale of triage infrastructure. OpenClaw is the only project in this set with a formalized triage taxonomy ("clawsweeper" ratings: gold shrimp → platinum hermit, fix-shape, needs-info flags). This is a mature workflow artifact no peer exhibits.
  • Breadth of channel surface. Telegram, Slack, msteams, Codex, claude-cli — the integration matrix is wider than any peer, at the cost of more seams to break.
  • Ecosystem gravity. 333 issues / 500 PRs in 24h is roughly an order of magnitude above Hermes Agent (50/50), QwenPaw (20/36), and ZeroClaw (7/50). OpenClaw is functioning as the de facto reference implementation of the category.

Technical approach differences:

  • Unlike QwenPaw (release-driven, channel-plugin model) or ZeroClaw (Rust, sandbox/relay-centric arc), OpenClaw leans on a JavaScript/TypeScript gateway + plugin architecture with heavy reliance on a SQLite worker layer and a Gateway event loop. This is precisely where its dominant failure families live — event-loop blocking at scale (#119720, open since August), SQLite worker OOM (#191847), and off-heap RSS creep (#182369). Peers architecturally sidestep or defer some of this pressure (ZeroClaw's Rust runtime, QwenPaw's per-channel isolation).
  • OpenClaw's access-control model (OpenClaw ID: member/guest/admin/Doctor roles via stacked PRs) is more ambitious and further along than peers' — but it also means OpenClaw carries more security surface area in-flight.

Community size comparison:

  • Largest by raw engagement: OpenClaw's hottest thread (#170956, Windows lifecycle) drew 32 comments; its top six threads average ~19 comments. Compare to QwenPaw's top thread (#8071, 13 comments) and Hermes Agent's hottest (#77253, 13 comments). OpenClaw's community comments in aggregate on a single issue can exceed a peer's entire daily comment volume.
  • The trade-off is visible: OpenClaw's maintainer bandwidth is the binding constraint — several fixes exist on main but not in stable (e.g., #177063→#185085), producing a release-velocity gap that Hermes Agent (canary-per-day cadence) and QwenPaw (fix-PR-within-24h culture) avoid.

Net position: OpenClaw is the ecosystem's anchor reference but currently pays a heavy reliability tax for its scope. A stable-backport push would likely reduce user-visible P1 volume more than net-new development this cycle — a low-cost, high-leverage move peers have already internalized.

4. Shared Technical Focus Areas

Three requirements emerge independently across multiple projects — the strongest signal in this dataset:

(a) Silent data/delivery loss — the #1 cross-project reliability theme

  • OpenClaw: Subagent final answer lost + duplicate settle events (#155119); exec-completion wakes lost (#185085); Telegram opaque callbacks dropped (#126950); Slack thread-mismatch.
  • Hermes Agent: notify_on_complete stale synthetic turn (#94455, closed today); background work fails to follow through (#149248 — "nearly every time I've asked Hermes to handle something long-running… it hasn't come back"); session_search silently returns 0 (#103184).
  • Shared root cause: asynchronous gateway/session state races at the plugin↔core boundary. Multiple projects independently report the same class of bug — a strong signal this is an architectural pattern, not a project-specific defect.

(b) Security boundaries that are either too blunt or bypassable

  • Hermes Agent: E.164 phone-number over-redaction (#68911, needs-decision); ANSI-C quoting approval bypass (#76218, closed); skill egress over-blocking (#143863).
  • ZeroClaw: Caller tool-level approval in bounded delegation (#11138); MITM egress proxy RFC (#12001); write-only credential management (#12373); /mnt/UNC denylist tightening (#12136, breaking).
  • OpenClaw: Unbypassable outbound policy enforcement (#56349, open since March); exec approval card fails to flag mount-point targets (#124306).
  • Shared need: a coherent, auditable model for delegated authority and secret visibility — users want to constrain a compromised agent, not just a misbehaving one.

(c) Provider/model configuration trust

  • QwenPaw: Hub model gateway 502 on Anthropic/MiniMax presets (#8718); context-length exceeded → task aborts (#8312); in-channel /model cannot switch pinned model (#8725).
  • ZeroClaw: OpenCode Go silently using Zen's catalogue (#12412); context-window discovery returns nothing (#12413).
  • OpenClaw: Codex provider/thread mismatch regression (#190563); claude-cli treats transient OAuth refresh-lock as terminal (#156442).
  • Shared need: predictable, inspectable model selection — users are losing trust when providers silently mismatch catalogues or fail opaque.

(d) CJK/i18n gaps (currently OpenClaw-specific but a category-level risk)

  • OpenClaw: CJK bigram tokenizer (#170997) and sessions_search returning 0 for CJK (#140736). No peer has surfaced this yet — a signal that other projects are under-serving non-English users, likely a latent issue as adoption grows.

5. Differentiation Analysis

Dimension OpenClaw Hermes Agent ZeroClaw QwenPaw IronClaw
Primary focus Broadest channel + access-control platform Security hardening + gateway/session reliability Rust sandbox/relay + credential scoping Channel-plugin ecosystem (WeChat/Feishu/DingTalk/Matrix) Niche/org-specific (nearai)
Target users Power users, multi-channel operators Security-conscious ops + desktop users Security-literate, multi-agent builders Messaging-first users (CJK-adjacent markets) Specialized/internal
Architecture signal TS/JS gateway + plugin + SQLite worker Gateway + canary cadence; desktop TUI Rust runtime, WASM plugins, relay/frontdoor, Seatbelt Console/API + channel plugin model (not visible today)
Release cadence Slow stable, huge main drift Canary-per-day, stable periodic v0.9.0 pending Post-2.3.0 fix wave Idle
Security posture Ambitious in-flight (access model) Explicit "sec-marathon" campaign Architectural (MITM proxy, write-only secrets) Reactive (regression fixes) CI-hardening proposal only
Distinct pain Windows lifecycle, event-loop scale Desktop rendering, gateway concurrency Provider catalogue confusion, identity leakage Upgrade migration gaps, channel startup races None surfaced

Key architectural divergence: ZeroClaw is the only project systematically moving security from "policy" to "architecture" (MITM egress proxy, host-mediated WASM wake dispatch via ADR-016, write-only secret vault pattern). Hermes Agent pursues similar goals through enforcement fixes (peeling exec wrappers before MCP scans, gating instruction files). OpenClaw approaches security through role-based access semantics. These are three genuinely different philosophies — worth watching which becomes the ecosystem norm.

6. Community Momentum & Maturity

Activity tiers:

  • Tier 1 — Hyperactive reference platform: OpenClaw (333 issues / 500 PRs). Mature triage workflow, but stability debt and release-velocity gap.
  • Tier 2 — High-velocity, healthy flow: Hermes Agent (50/50, 12 merged, canary cut) and ZeroClaw (7/50, but 49 open — volume without closure). Both security-marathon-driven.
  • Tier 2.5 — Responsive post-release stabilizer: QwenPaw (20/36, 5 merged, fast issue→fix turnaround within 24h). High contributor responsiveness, absorbing 2.3.0 regressions.
  • Tier 3 — Idle/niche: IronClaw (1 issue, 0 PRs, 0 releases).

Rapidly iterating: OpenClaw (features + fixes in parallel), QwenPaw (most active contributor conversion — first-time contributors turning reports into fixes, e.g., #8728, #8726).

Stabilizing / absorbing regressions: QwenPaw is in explicit post-release stabilization; ZeroClaw is in a review-phase stall (49 open PRs, several needs-author-action — a healthier failure mode than maintainer bottleneck, but still slowing the hardening pipeline).

Maturity signals ranked:

  1. OpenClaw — most mature tooling (clawsweeper taxonomy), largest community, but lowest flow efficiency (backlog accumulation).
  2. Hermes Agent — highest sustainable maturity: balanced flow, daily canary cadence, security campaign closing bugs same-day.
  3. ZeroClaw — high architectural ambition, high contributor sophistication, but review throughput is the visible weakness (#9746 open since August).
  4. QwenPaw — maturing fast; plugin ecosystem pressure (#8071, 13 comments) is a good sign of ecosystem depth beyond core.
  5. IronClaw — cannot be assessed from a single-day trough; the unanswered #8170 (a high-quality CI-hardening contribution) is a risk of squandered low-cost engagement.

7. Trend Signals

Extracted from cross-project community feedback — actionable for AI agent developers:

1. Delivery reliability is the new feature bar. Across OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and QwenPaw, silent loss of background/long-running work is the highest-emotion complaint ("hasn't come back," "stuck pending," "task aborts"). Developers should treat durable, observable async delivery with explicit acknowledgment/retry as a first-class primitive, not an afterthought. The recurring deliveryStatus/notify_on_complete/session_search family suggests the industry lacks a standard contract here.

2. Gateway event-loop/state concurrency is an architectural ceiling. OpenClaw (#119720, #182369) and Hermes Agent (#94455, #149248) independently hit session-state races and memory pressure under scale. For new projects: isolate persistence from the serving loop early (ZeroClaw's Rust runtime and QwenPaw's channel isolation offer partial templates). Retrofitting is expensive — OpenClaw has carried #119720 since August.

3. The security model is shifting from "policy" to "isolation." The most forward-looking proposals (ZeroClaw MITM proxy, write-only secrets, bounded-delegation approval; Hermes exec-wrapper peeling; OpenClaw unbypassable outbound policy) all point the same direction: assume agent compromise, not just agent misbehavior. Developers building multi-agent/tool-using systems should design secret-visibility boundaries and delegation-approval inheritance upfront — this is becoming table stakes, not enterprise upsell.

4. Over-blocking is as damaging as under-blocking. User pain is now bidirectional: redaction that hides legitimate E.164 numbers (#68911), skill egress blocks that kill documented curl calls (#143863). Design per-profile/per-skill exceptions into security primitives from day one. The "guard too blunt" refrain is a predictable second-order effect of security hardening — plan for the tuning surface.

5. Provider abstraction is a trust surface. Silent catalogue mismatches (ZeroClaw/Zen-vs-Go), context-window discovery failures, and opaque model pinning (QwenPaw #8725) erode user trust. Ship inspectable provider resolution (what catalogue, which context window, why this model) and self-recovery paths.

6. Release cadence is a reliability lever, not just a marketing event. OpenClaw's fixes sitting on main but absent from stable (#177063→#185085) directly inflate user-visible P1 volume. Hermes Agent's canary-per-day cadence keeps fixes in user hands fast. Stable backporting is a higher-ROI activity than net-new features for projects at OpenClaw's scale — a directly transferable lesson.

7. Non-English support is a latent, underserved risk. Only OpenClaw surfaces CJK tokenization problems — which may mean peers simply haven't been stress-tested by CJK-heavy users yet. Given QwenPaw's messaging-channel focus (WeChat/Feishu/DingTalk), expect i18n search/tokenization to become a cross-project requirement in the next two quarters.

8. First-time contributors are a strategic asset. QwenPaw's fast issue→fix conversion (first-time contributors filing PRs for #8718, #8727, #8709 within 24h) illustrates the highest-leverage community pattern. IronClaw's unanswered #8170 (a specific, low-cost, high-quality contribution) is the counter-example: squandering a willing contributor is a compounding cost. Projects should instrument "time-to-first-response on external contributions" as a health metric.

Bottom line for decision-makers: The category is consolidating around reliability + security semantics rather than feature breadth. OpenClaw leads in scale and integration surface but pays for it in stability debt and release lag; Hermes Agent and ZeroClaw demonstrate that flow efficiency and architectural security can be competitive advantages even at lower volume; QwenPaw shows that responsive maintainership converts release regressions into community goodwill. The next 1–2 release cycles will likely be decided less by who ships the most features and more by who reliably delivers background work, keeps secrets out of agent reach, and gets fixes into stable fastest.

  • PR #9746 — per-agent ownership scoping for session tools and discord_search. Open since 2026-08-04 (~3+ months), priority:p1, risk:high, distinguished contributor, needs-author-action, XL. Touches identity-access, memory backend, channel core/telegram/discord. Long-lived and high-impact — deserves a clear path to merge or a decision.
  • PR #12140 and PR #12136 — both risk:high, needs-author-action; #12136 is breaking. They've been open since late October; breaking security changes need timely review to avoid stale rebases and surprise breakage.
  • PR #12240 — cron --agent reassignment persistence, risk:high, needs-author-action (since 2026-11-05). A correctness fix that's quietly waiting.
  • Issue #11138 — status:accepted but still open since 2026-09-26; the delegation-approval design needs a resolution to unblock dependent work.

Note: The needs-author-action label appears on several high-risk PRs — the bottleneck here is author response, not maintainer review, which is a healthier failure mode but still slows the security-hardening pipeline.
